content.text: Xuanzang (Hiuen Tsiang) was born in A.D. 603 at Ch'in Liu in the province of Ho-nan, the youngest of four brothers. Taken as a boy by his second brother, a monk, to the eastern capital Lo-yang, he was ordained at the Tsing-tu temple at the age of thirteen. Amid the troubles at the end of the Sui dynasty he fled with his brother to Shu-chu, capital of Sz'chuen, where at the age of twenty he was fully ordained as a Bhikshu.
content.source_name: Samuel Beal (trans.), Si-Yu-Ki: Buddhist Records of the Western World (1884), Introduction (d): Hiuen Tsiang or Xuanzang

content.text: Travelling through the provinces in search of the best instructors he could find, Xuanzang came at length to Chang'an. There, stirred by the memory of the earlier pilgrims Fa-hian and Chi-yen, he resolved, at twenty-six years of age, to journey to the western regions to question the sages on points that troubled his mind — setting out from Chang'an in the company of a fellow priest.
content.source_name: Samuel Beal (trans.), Si-Yu-Ki: Buddhist Records of the Western World (1884), Introduction (d): Hiuen Tsiang or Xuanzang

content.text: At Liang-chau, the entrepot for merchants from Tibet and beyond the Tsung-ling mountains, Xuanzang explained the sacred books and revealed his purpose of travelling to the kingdom of the Brahmans to seek the Law. Provided with means for his journey by grateful merchants, and 'notwithstanding the expostulation of the governor of the city,' he was able, through the connivance of two priests, to press onward westward as far as Kwa-chau — defying official efforts to stop him.
content.source_name: Samuel Beal (trans.), Si-Yu-Ki: Buddhist Records of the Western World (1884), Introduction (d): Hiuen Tsiang or Xuanzang

content.text: Going north with a young guide who had offered to lead him, Xuanzang crossed a river by night and, after escaping the treachery of that very guide, came on alone to the first of five watch-towers stretching toward the country of I-gu (Kamul), spaced at intervals of a hundred li. The text notes, without needing to recount every detail, 'the fervent prayers to Kwan-yin and his incessant invocation of the name of this divinity' by which the lone pilgrim sustained himself through the crossing.
content.source_name: Samuel Beal (trans.), Si-Yu-Ki: Buddhist Records of the Western World (1884), Introduction (d): Hiuen Tsiang or Xuanzang

content.text: Having prevailed on the keepers of the first and fourth watch-towers to let him pass, Xuanzang at last reached the confines of I-gu and halted there — only to be summoned by the prince of Kao-chang (Turfan), who attempted in vain to keep the pilgrim in his territory before finally releasing him onward toward 'O-ki-ni (Karasharh) and the long road to India via Kuche, the Icy Mountains, and the valley of the Chu river.
content.source_name: Samuel Beal (trans.), Si-Yu-Ki: Buddhist Records of the Western World (1884), Introduction (d): Hiuen Tsiang or Xuanzang

content.text: Xuanzang had been away from China since A.D. 629; he returned in A.D. 645, having crossed the Pamir and passed back through Kashgar and Khotan. He brought with him five hundred grains of relics of the Buddha's body, seven statues of the Buddha in gold, silver, and sandalwood, one hundred and twenty-four works of the Great Vehicle, and other texts amounting to 520 fascicles — carried, the record notes, by twenty-two horses.
content.source_name: Samuel Beal (trans.), Si-Yu-Ki: Buddhist Records of the Western World (1884), Introduction (d): Hiuen Tsiang or Xuanzang

content.text: Of the many books Xuanzang translated after his return, seventy-five still survive within the collection of the Chinese Tripitaka. His travel record, the Si-Yu-Ki, together with the biography written by his disciple Hwui-lih, preserved for posterity a first-hand account of Buddhist India in the seventh century that remains a primary historical source to this day.
content.source_name: Samuel Beal (trans.), Si-Yu-Ki: Buddhist Records of the Western World (1884), Introduction (d): Hiuen Tsiang or Xuanzang
